newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages sing and pray, Japan fears errors.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages sing and pray, Japan fears errors.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis entered its 20th day on Monday with 74 hostages held by Marxist rebels praying and singing for freedom but little sign their wishes would be granted anytime soon.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he feared the deadlocked situation at the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador in Lima could get out of hand with the slightest slip by either the Peruvian government or the rebels.
"It will be a protracted battle, and situations like that make me worried about an unexpected accident," Hashimoto told reporters at his official residence on Monday.
"There have been miscues on the guerrillas' side and also on the the Peruvian government's side," he said without elaborating.
Hashimoto has firmly stressed since the outset of the hostage crisis that Tokyo wants a peaceful outcome and has also expressed fears that a dramatic rescue attempt could cause bloodshed.

Hashimoto, who cancelled New Year plans so he could monitor the hostage crisis, on Tuesday will begin a trip to five Southeast Asian countries, a move officials said reflected Japan's confidence in the government of Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori.
"We will continue to place absolute trust in the Peruvian government and handle the crisis carefully," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said.
The hostages, seeking to boost morale after four days without a single person's release, sang on Sunday about returning home.
"I want to return, return, return to my home once again," they sang by candlelight to the tune of a Mexican folk melody.
The chorus of another song ran: "Sing, and don't cry."
Witnesses said female voices could be heard joining in, indicating that two teenage rebel girls -- the only women left inside the residence -- were singing along. Women's laughter was also heard.

About 20 rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) are holding 74 people, including two ambassadors, more than a dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, top Peruvian officials and Fujimori's brother Pedro.

Earlier on Sunday Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani celebrated Mass inside the residence and Pope John Paul II, in an apparent appeal to the MRTA rebels, urged kidnappers to free their captives as a "gesture of humanity."

"The mercy of Christ, born of human weakness, urges hostage-takers to fulfil this gesture of humanity -- free these people," the pope told pilgrims in St Peter's Square during his regular Sunday address.

Other than Cipriani's visit, the only activity at the mined and booby-trapped residence was the routine visits of Red Cross officials bearing medicines, food and other supplies such as books, cleaning materials and cigarettes.

The guerrillas have not released any hostages since New Year's Day, and Fujimori's negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, has not entered the residence since a first face-to-face meeting eight days ago.
Neither side relaxed its uncompromising position, with the heavily armed MRTA rebels maintaining a demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades and Fujimori flatly refusing.
Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar arrived in Lima on Sunday to try to help bring about a solution. Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio is among the captives.
At a news conference, Aranibar backed Fujimori's uncompromising position and ruled out releasing four MRTA prisoners in Bolivia.
The standoff began Dec. 17 when the rebels burst in to a cocktail party honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday that was attended by more than 500 people.
They have since released about 430 of the original hostages.
